{{Short description|Random matrix with gaussian entries}}

In [[Random matrix|random matrix theory]], the '''Gaussian ensembles''' are specific [[probability distribution]]s over [[Hermitian matrix|self-adjoint matrices]] whose entries are independently sampled from the [[Normal distribution|gaussian distribution]]. They are among the most-commonly studied matrix ensembles, fundamental to both mathematics and physics. The three main examples are the Gaussian orthogonal (GOE), unitary (GUE), and symplectic (GSE) ensembles. These are classified by the [[Freeman Dyson|Dyson]] index ''β'', which takes values 1, 2, and 4 respectively, counting the number of real components per matrix element (1 for real elements, 2 for complex elements, 4 for [[quaternions]]). The index can be extended to take any real positive value.

The gaussian ensembles are also called the '''Wigner ensembles''',<ref>{{harv|Potters|Bouchaud|2020}}</ref> or the '''Hermite ensembles'''.<ref name="link.springer.com">{{Cite journal |last1=Edelman |first1=Alan |last2=Sutton |first2=Brian D. |date=June 2007 |title=From Random Matrices to Stochastic Operators |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10955-006-9226-4 |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |language=en |volume=127 |issue=6 |pages=1121–1165 |doi=10.1007/s10955-006-9226-4 |arxiv=math-ph/0607038 |bibcode=2007JSP...127.1121E |issn=0022-4715}}</ref>

== Definitions ==

=== Conventions ===
There are many conventions for defining the Gaussian ensembles. In this article, we specify exactly one of them.

In all definitions, the Gaussian ensemble have zero [[Expected value|expectation]].

* <math>\beta</math>: a positive real number. Called the '''Dyson index'''. The cases of <math>\beta = 1, 2, 4</math> are special.
* <math>N</math>: the side-length of a matrix. Always a positive integer.
* <math>W_{N}</math>: a matrix sampled from a Gaussian ensemble with size <math>N \times N</math>. The letter <math>W</math> stands for "Wigner".
* <math>M^*</math>: the [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] of a matrix. We assume <math>W_N = W_N^*</math> ([[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]]) when <math>W_{N}</math> is sampled from a gaussian ensemble.
** If <math>M</math> is real, then <math>M^*</math> is its [[transpose]].
** If <math>M</math> is complex or quaternionic, then <math>M^*</math> is its [[conjugate transpose]].
* <math>\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N</math>: the [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] of the matrix, which are all real, since the matrices are always assumed to be self-adjoint.
* <math>\sigma_{d}^2</math>: the variance of on-diagonal matrix entries. We assume that for each <math>N</math>, all on-diagonal matrix entries have the same variance. It is always defined as <math>\mathbb E[|W_{N, }|^2]</math>. 
* <math>\sigma_{od}^2</math>: the variance of off-diagonal matrix entries. We assume that for each <math>N</math>, all off-diagonal matrix entries have the same variance. It is always defined as <math>\mathbb E[|W_{N, ij}|^2]</math> where <math>i \neq j</math>.
** For a complex number, <math>|a + bi|^2 = a^2 + b^2</math>.
** For a [[quaternion]], <math>|a + bi + cj + dk|^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2</math>.
* <math> Z </math>: the [[Partition function (mathematics)|partition function]].

There are equivalent definitions for the GβE(N) ensembles, given below.

=== By sampling ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, the GβE(N) ensemble is defined by how it is sampled:

* Sample a gaussian matrix <math> X_N </math>, such that all its entries are [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|IID]] sampled from the corresponding standard normal distribution.
** If <math> \beta = 1 </math>, then <math> X_{N, ij} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1) </math>.
** If <math> \beta = 2 </math>, then <math> X_{N, ij} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/2) + i\mathcal N(0, 1/2) </math>.
** If <math> \beta = 4 </math>, then <math> X_{N, ij} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/4) + i\mathcal N(0, 1/4) + j\mathcal N(0, 1/4) + k\mathcal N(0, 1/4)  </math>.
* Let <math> W_N = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(X + X^*) </math>.

=== By density ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, the GβE(N) ensemble is defined with density function <math display="block">\rho(W_N) = \frac{1}{Z} e^{- \frac{\beta}{4}\sum_{i = 1}^N W_{N, ii}^2 - \frac \beta 2 \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |W_{N, ij}|^2} = \frac{1}{Z} e^{- \frac{\beta}{4} \mathrm{Tr} W_N^2}</math>where the partition function is <math>
Z = 2^{\frac 12 N}\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\right)^{\frac 12 N + \frac 14 \beta N (N-1)}</math>.

The '''Gaussian orthogonal ensemble''' GOE(N) is defined as the probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> symmetric matrices with density function<math display="block">\rho(W_N) = \frac{1}{Z} e^{- \frac{1}{4}\sum_{i = 1}^N W_{N, ii}^2 - \frac 12 \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} W_{N, ij}^2} = \frac{1}{Z} e^{- \frac{1}{4} \mathrm{Tr} W_N^2} </math>where the partition function is <math>
Z = 2^{\frac{1}{4}N(N+3)}\pi^{\frac{1}{4}N(N+1)}</math>.

Explicitly, since there are only <math>\frac 12 N(N+1)</math> degrees of freedom, the parameterization is as follows:<math display="block">\rho(W_N) \prod_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq N} dW_{N, ij} </math>where we pick the upper diagonal entries <math>\{W_{ij}\}_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq N}</math> as the degrees of freedom.

The '''Gaussian unitary ensemble''' GUE(N) is defined as the probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> Hermitian matrices with density function<math display="block">
\rho(W_N)
  = \frac{1}{Z}
    e^{-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i = 1}^N W_{N, ii}^2
       - \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |W_{N, ij}|^2}
  = \frac{1}{Z} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\,W_N^2}.
</math>where the partition function is <math>Z = 2^{\frac{1}{2}N}\pi^{\frac{1}{2}N^{2}}</math>.

Explicitly, since there are only <math>N^{2}</math> degrees of freedom, the parameterization is as follows:
<math display="block">
\rho(W_N)\,
\prod_{i = 1}^{N} dW_{N, ii}\;
\prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N}
      d(\mathrm{Re}\,W_{N, ij})\,
      d(\mathrm{Im}\,W_{N, ij})
</math>where we pick the upper diagonal entries <math>\{W_{N, ii}\}_{1 \leq i \leq N} \cup
      \{\mathrm{Re}\,W_{N, ij},\,
        \mathrm{Im}\,W_{N, ij}\}_{1 \leq i < j \leq N}</math> as the degrees of freedom.

The '''Gaussian symplectic ensemble''' GSE(N) is defined as the probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> self‑adjoint quaternionic matrices with density function<math display="block">
\rho(W_N)
  = \frac{1}{Z}
    e^{- \sum_{i = 1}^N W_{N, ii}^2
       - 2 \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |W_{N, ij}|^2}
  = \frac{1}{Z} e^{-\mathrm{Tr}\,W_N^2}.
</math>where the partition function is <math>Z = 2^{-N(N-1)}\pi^{\frac{1}{2}N(2N-1)}</math>.

Explicitly, since there are only <math>N(2N - 1)</math> degrees of freedom, the parameterization is as follows:<math display="block">
\rho(W_N)\,
\prod_{i = 1}^{N} dW_{N, ii}\;
\prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N}
      \prod_{a = 0}^{3} dW_{N, ij}^{(a)}
</math>where we write <math>W_{N, ij} = W_{N, ij}^{(0)}
                + i\,W_{N, ij}^{(1)}
                + j\,W_{N, ij}^{(2)}
                + k\,W_{N, ij}^{(3)}</math> and pick the upper diagonal entries <math>\{W_{N, ii}\}_{1 \leq i \leq N} \cup
      \{W_{N, ij}^{(a)}\}_{1 \leq i < j \leq N,\;0 \leq a \leq 3}</math> as the degrees of freedom.

=== By invariance ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, the GβE(N) ensemble is uniquely characterized (up to [[Affine transformation|affine transform]]) by its symmetries, or invariance under appropriate transformations.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Mehta|2004|loc=Def 2.3.1, 2.4.1, 2.5.1}}</ref>

For GOE, consider a probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> symmetric matrices satisfying the following properties:

* Invariance under [[orthogonal transformation]]: For any fixed (not random) <math>N \times N</math> [[orthogonal matrix]] <math>O</math>, let <math>M</math> be a random sample from the distribution. Then <math>OMO^T</math> has the same distribution as <math>M</math>.
* [[Independence (probability theory)|Independence]]: The entries <math>\{M_{ij}\}_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq N}</math> are independently distributed.

For GUE, consider a probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> Hermitian matrices satisfying the following properties:

* Invariance under [[unitary transformation]]: For any fixed (not random) <math>N \times N</math> [[unitary matrix]] <math>U</math>, let <math>M</math> be a random sample from the distribution. Then <math>UMU^*</math> has the same distribution as <math>M</math>.
* Independence: The entries <math>\{M_{ij}\}_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq N}</math> are independently distributed.

For GSE, consider a probability distribution over <math>N \times N</math> self-adjoint quaternionic matrices satisfying the following properties:

* Invariance under [[symplectic transformation]]: For any fixed (not random) <math>N \times N</math> [[symplectic matrix]] <math>S</math>, let <math>M</math> be a random sample from the distribution. Then <math>SMS^*</math> has the same distribution as <math>M</math>.
* Independence: The entries <math>\{M_{ij}\}_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq N}</math> are independently distributed.

In all 3 cases, these conditions force the distribution to have the form <math>\rho(M) = \frac 1Z e^{- a \operatorname{Tr}(M^2) + b \operatorname{Tr}(M)}</math>, where <math>a > 0</math> and <math>b, Z \in \R</math>. Thus, with the further specification of <math>\frac 1N \mathbb E[\operatorname{Tr}(M)] = 0, \frac{1}{N^2} \mathbb E[\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)] = 1 + \frac{2/\beta - 1}{N}</math>, we recover the GOE, GUE, GSE.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Mehta|2004|loc=Thm. 2.6.3}}</ref> Notably, if mere invariance is demanded, then any spectral distribution can be produced by multiplying with a function of form <math>f(\operatorname{Tr}(X), \operatorname{Tr}(X^2), \operatorname{Tr}(X^3), \dots)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wigner |first=Eugene P. |date=January 1967 |title=Random Matrices in Physics |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1009001 |journal=SIAM Review |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.1137/1009001 |bibcode=1967SIAMR...9....1W |issn=0036-1445|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

More succinctly stated, each of GOE, GUE, GSE is uniquely specified by invariance, independence, the mean, and the variance.

=== By spectral distribution ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, the GβE(N) ensemble is defined as the ensemble obtained by <math>ADA^*</math>, where

* <math>D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)</math> is a diagonal real matrix with its entries sampled according to the spectral density, defined below;
* <math>A</math> is an orthogonal/unitary/symplectic matrix sampled uniformly, that is, from the normalized [[Haar measure]] of the [[Orthogonal group|orthogonal]]/[[Unitary group|unitary]]/[[Symplectic group|symplectic]] group.
In this way, the GβE(N) ensemble may be defined after the spectral density is defined first, so that any method to motivate the spectral density then motivates the GβE(N) ensemble, and vice versa.

=== By maximal entropy ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, the GβE(N) ensemble is uniquely characterized as the absolutely continuous probability distribution <math>\rho</math> over <math>N\times N</math> real/complex/quaternionic symmetric/orthogonal/symplectic matrices that [[Principle of maximum entropy|maximizes entropy]] <math>\mathbb E_{M \sim \rho}[- \ln \rho(M)]</math>, under the constraint of <math>\frac{1}{N^2}\mathbb E_{M \sim \rho}[\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)] = 1 + \frac{2/\beta - 1}{N} </math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Toscano |first1=Fabricio |last2=Vallejos |first2=Raúl O. |last3=Tsallis |first3=Constantino |date=2004-06-17 |title=Random matrix ensembles from nonextensive entropy |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.69.066131 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=69 |issue=6 |article-number=066131 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.69.066131|pmid=15244691 |arxiv=cond-mat/0402215 |bibcode=2004PhRvE..69f6131T }}</ref>

== Spectral density ==
For eigenvalues <math>\lambda_{1}, \dots, \lambda_{N}</math> the joint density of G''β''E(N) is<math display="block">\rho_{\beta, N}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N) = \frac{1}{Z_{\beta, N}} e^{-\frac \beta 4 \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i^2} \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |\lambda_i - \lambda_j|^\beta = \frac{1}{Z_{\beta, N}} e^{-\frac{\beta}{4}\|\lambda\|_{2}^{2}} |\Delta_{N}(\lambda)|^{\beta}</math>where <math>\Delta_{N}</math> is the [[Vandermonde determinant]], and the partition function <math>Z_{\beta, N}</math> is explicitly evaluated as a [[Selberg integral]]:<ref>{{Harvard citation|Mehta|2004|loc=Thm. 3.3.1}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{aligned}
Z_{\beta, N} &= \int_{\R^N} e^{-\frac \beta 4 \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i^2} \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |\lambda_i - \lambda_j|^\beta d\lambda\\
&= (2\pi)^{\frac N2} \left(\frac 2\beta\right)^{\frac 12N + \frac  14 \beta N(N-1)} \prod_{j=1}^N \frac{\Gamma\left(1 + j\frac \beta 2\right)}{\Gamma\left(1 + \frac \beta 2\right)}
\end{aligned}</math>where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Gamma function|Euler Gamma function]]. The expression is particularly simple when <math>\beta = 2</math>, where we have a [[superfactorial]]:<math display="block">Z_{2, N} = (2\pi)^{\frac N2}\prod_{j=1}^N j!</math>

=== Determinantal point process ===
[[File:Spectral density of GUE, N = 1 to 32.png|thumb|Histogram of the empirical spectral density of <math>\frac 1\sqrt N W_N</math> for <math>2^0, \dots, 2^5</math>, obtained by averaging over <math>10^5</math> samples of the matrix, compared with the theoretical prediction of <math>\sqrt N \rho(\sqrt N x)</math>.]]
Define functions <math>\psi_n(x) := \frac{e^{-\frac 14 x^2}}{\sqrt{n!\sqrt{2\pi}}} \operatorname{He}_n(x)</math>, where <math>\operatorname{He}</math> is the [[Probabilist's Hermite polynomials|probabilist's Hermite polynomial]]. These are the [[Wave function|wavefunction]] states of the [[quantum harmonic oscillator]].

The spectrum of GUE(N) is a [[determinantal point process]] with kernel <math>K_N(x, x') := \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \psi_n(x) \psi_n(x')</math>, and by the [[Christoffel–Darboux formula]],<math display="block">K_N(x, x') = \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{4}\left(x^2+x^{\prime 2}\right)}}{(N-1)!\sqrt{2 \pi}} \frac{\operatorname{He}_N(x) \operatorname{He}_{N-1}\left(x^{\prime}\right)-\operatorname{He}_{N-1}(x) \operatorname{He}_N\left(x^{\prime}\right)}{x-x^{\prime}}</math>Using the confluent form of Christoffel–Darboux and the three-term recurrence of Hermite polynomials, the spectral density of GUE(N) for finite values of <math>N</math>:<ref>{{harv|Livan|Novaes|Vivo|2018|loc=Chap. 10}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\rho(x) &= \frac 1N K_N(x,x)  \\
&= \frac{1}{N\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac 12 x^2} \sum_{n = 0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{n!} \operatorname{He}_n(x)^2 \\
&= \frac{e^{-x^2 / 2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi}N!}\left(\operatorname{He}_{N}(x)^2 - \operatorname{He}_{N+1}(x) \operatorname{He}_{N-1}(x)\right)
\end{aligned}</math>The spectral distribution of <math>\beta = 1, 4</math> can also be written as a ''quaternionic'' determinantal point process involving skew-orthogonal polynomials.<ref>{{harv|Livan|Novaes|Vivo|2018|loc=Chap. 12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Adler |first1=M. |last2=Forrester |first2=P. J. |last3=Nagao |first3=T. |last4=van Moerbeke |first4=P. |date=2000-04-01 |title=Classical Skew Orthogonal Polynomials and Random Matrices |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |language=en |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=141–170 |doi=10.1023/A:1018644606835 |arxiv=solv-int/9907001 |bibcode=2000JSP....99..141A |issn=1572-9613}}</ref>

=== Tridiagonalization ===
For all <math> \beta = 1, 2, 4 </math> cases, given a sampled matrix <math>W_N</math> from the GβE(N) ensemble, we can perform a [[Hessenberg matrix#Householder transformations|Householder transformation tridiagonalization]] on it to obtain a [[tridiagonal matrix]] <math>T_{\beta, N}</math>, which has the same distribution as<math display="block">\sqrt{\frac 1\beta}\begin{bmatrix}
a_N\sqrt2 & b_{N-1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
b_{N-1} & a_{N-1}\sqrt2 & b_{N-2} & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & b_{N-2} & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \ddots & a_{2}\sqrt2 & b_1 \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & b_1 & a_1 \sqrt2
\end{bmatrix} </math>where each <math>a_{1}, \dots, a_{N} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)</math> is gaussian-distributed, and each <math>b_i \sim \chi_{i\beta }</math> is [[Chi distribution|chi-distributed]], and all <math>a_{1}, \dots, a_{N}, b_{1}, \dots, b_{N-1}</math> are independent. The <math> \beta = 1 </math> case was first noted in 1984,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Trotter |first=Hale F. |date=October 1984 |title=Eigenvalue distributions of large Hermitian matrices; Wigner's semi-circle law and a theorem of Kac, Murdock, and Szegö |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |language=en |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=67–82 |doi=10.1016/0001-8708(84)90037-9|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the general case was noted in 2002.<ref name=":0" /> Like how the [[Laplace operator|Laplace differential operator]] can be discretized to the [[Laplacian matrix]], this tridiagonal form of the gaussian ensemble allows a reinterpretation of the gaussian ensembles as an ensemble over not matrices, but over [[differential operator]]s, specifically, a "stochastic Airy operator". This leads more generally to the study of random matrices as stochastic operators.<ref name="link.springer.com"/>

Computationally, this allows efficient sampling of eigenvalues, from <math>O(N^3)</math> on the full matrix, to just <math>O(N^2)</math> on the tridiagonal matrix. If one only requires a histogram of the eigenvalues with <math>m</math> bins, the time can be further decreased to <math>O(Nm)</math>, by using the [[Sturm's theorem|Sturm sequences]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Albrecht |first1=James T. |last2=Chan |first2=Cy P. |last3=Edelman |first3=Alan |date=2009-08-01 |title=Sturm Sequences and Random Eigenvalue Distributions |journal=Foundations of Computational Mathematics |language=en |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=461–483 |doi=10.1007/s10208-008-9037-x |issn=1615-3383}}</ref> Theoretically, this definition allows extension to all <math> \beta > 0 </math> cases, leading to the gaussian [[beta ensemble]]s,<ref>{{Harvard citation|Forrester|2010|loc=Prop. 1.9.4}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Dumitriu |first1=Ioana |last2=Edelman |first2=Alan |date=2002-11-01 |title=Matrix models for beta ensembles |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=43 |issue=11 |pages=5830–5847 |doi=10.1063/1.1507823 |arxiv=math-ph/0206043 |bibcode=2002JMP....43.5830D |issn=0022-2488}}</ref> and "anti-symmetric" gaussian beta ensembles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dumitriu |first1=Ioana |last2=Forrester |first2=Peter J. |date=2010-09-01 |title=Tridiagonal realization of the antisymmetric Gaussian β-ensemble |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/51/9/093302/896718/Tridiagonal-realization-of-the-antisymmetric |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=51 |issue=9 |doi=10.1063/1.3486071 |arxiv=0904.2216 |bibcode=2010JMP....51i3302D |issn=0022-2488}}</ref>

Relatedly, let <math>X_N</math> be a <math>N\times N</math> matrix, with all entries IID sampled from the corresponding standard normal distribution – for example, if <math>\beta = 2</math>, then <math> X_{N, ij} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/2) + i\mathcal N(0, 1/2) </math>. Then applying repeated Housholder transform on only the left side of a results in <math>R_N = H_1 \dots H_N X_N</math>, where each <math>H_i</math> is a [[Householder matrix]], and <math>R_N</math> is an upper triangular matrix with independent entries, such that each <math>\sqrt{\beta}R_{N, ii} \sim \chi_{N+1-i}</math> for <math>1 \leq i \leq N</math>, and each <math>R_{N, ij} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/\beta)^{\otimes \beta}</math> for <math>1 \leq i < j \leq N</math>.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Edelman |first1=Alan |chapter=Random Matrix Theory and Its Innovative Applications |date=2013 |title=Advances in Applied Mathematics, Modeling, and Computational Science |pages=91–116 |editor-last=Melnik |editor-first=Roderick |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-5389-5_5 |isbn=978-1-4614-5389-5 |last2=Wang |first2=Yuyang |hdl=1721.1/115827 |editor2-last=Kotsireas |editor2-first=Ilias S.|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Global law ===
[[File:Spectral density of gaussian ensembels, N = 1 to 32.png|thumb|361x361px|Spectral density of GOE/GUE/GSE for <math>N = 2^{0}, 2^{1}, \dots, 2^{5}</math>. Each distribution is normalized to converge to the semicircle with radius 2.]]
The '''Wigner semicircle law''' states that the empirical eigenvalue distribution of <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}W_N </math> [[converges in distribution]] to the [[Wigner semicircle distribution]] with radius 2.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Tao|2012|loc=Thm. 2.4.2}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation|Forrester|2010|loc=Prop. 1.4.4}}</ref> That is, the distribution on <math>[-2, +2] </math> with probability density function <math display="block">\rho_{sc}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2\pi} </math>

The requirement that the matrix ensemble to be a gaussian ensemble is too strong for the Wigner semicircle law. Indeed, the theorem applies generally for much more generic matrix ensembles.

=== As Coulomb gas ===

The joint density <math>\rho_{\beta,N}</math> can be written as a [[Gibbs measure]]:<math display="block">\rho_{\beta,N} = \frac{1}{Z_{\beta, N}^{\text{CG}}}e^{-\beta E_N}</math>with the energy function (also called the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]]) <math>E_N = \frac 14 \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i^2 - \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} \ln |\lambda_i - \lambda_j|</math>. This can be interpreted physically as a [[Boltzmann distribution]] of a physical system consisting of <math>N</math> identical unit electric charges constrained to move on the real line, repelling each other via the two-dimensional [[Electric potential|Coulomb potential]] <math>-\ln |x - y|</math>, while being attracted to the origin via a quadratic potential <math>\frac 14 x^2</math>. This is the [[Coulomb gas]] model for the eigenvalues.

In the macroscopic limit, one rescales <math>\lambda_i=N^{1/2}x_i</math> and defines the empirical measure <math>\mu_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i}</math>, obtaining <math>E_N \approx \frac 12 N^2 \left(\mathcal E[\mu] + \frac 12 \ln N \right)</math>, where the [[Mean-field theory|mean-field]] functional <math display="block">\mathcal E[\mu]=\frac12\int_\R x^2 \mu(dx)-\iint_{\R^2} \ln|x-y| \mu(dx) \mu(dy)</math>yields the leading order <math>N^2</math> term in <math>\ln Z_{\beta,N}</math>, termed the Coulomb gas free energy. The Coulomb gas free energy is minimized by the Wigner semicircle law <math>d\mu_{sc}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}\sqrt{4-x^2}1_{\{|x|\le2\}}dx</math>, which gives the limiting eigenvalue density.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Tao|2012|loc=Sec. 2.6.3.}}</ref>

Alternatively, suppose that there exists a <math>\rho_b</math>, such that the quadratic electric potential can be recreated (up to an additive constant) via<math display="block">\int_{-2\sqrt{ N}}^{2\sqrt{ N}} -\ln |x-y| \rho_b(y) d y=\frac{1}{4}x^2 + C, \quad x \in[-2\sqrt{N}, 2\sqrt{N}] .</math>Then, imposing a fixed background negative electric charge of density <math>|\rho_b(y)|</math> exactly cancels out the electric repulsion between the freely moving positive charges. Such a function does exist: <math>\rho_b(y) = -\frac{\sqrt{4N - y^2}}{2N\pi}</math>, which can be found by solving an [[integral equation]]. This indicates that the Wigner semicircle distribution is the equilibrium distribution.<ref>{{harv|Livan|Novaes|Vivo|2018|loc=Sec. 5.2}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Forrester |first=Peter |chapter=Beta ensembles |date=2015-09-17 |title=The Oxford Handbook of Random Matrix Theory |pages=414–432 |editor-last=Akemann |editor-first=Gernot |publisher=Oxford University Press |doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198744191.013.20 |isbn=978-0-19-874419-1 |editor2-last=Baik |editor2-first=Jinho |editor3-last=Di Francesco |editor3-first=Philippe}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation|Forrester|2010|loc=Sec.1.4}}</ref>

Gaussian fluctuations about <math>\mu_{sc}</math> obtained by expanding <math>E_N</math> to second order produce the sine kernel in the bulk and the Airy kernel at the soft edge after proper rescaling.

=== Extreme value ===
The largest eigenvalue for GβE(N) follows the [[Tracy–Widom distribution]] after proper translation and scaling.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Chiani M |year=2014 |title=Distribution of the largest eigenvalue for real Wishart and Gaussian random matrices and a simple approximation for the Tracy–Widom distribution |journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis |volume=129 |pages=69–81 |arxiv=1209.3394 |doi=10.1016/j.jmva.2014.04.002 |s2cid=15889291}}</ref> It can be efficiently sampled by the shift-invert Lanczos algorithm on the <math>10 n^{1/3} \times 10 n^{1/3}</math> upper left corner of the [[Gaussian ensemble#Tridiagonalization|tridiagonal matrix form]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Edelman |first1=Alan |last2=Rao |first2=N. Raj |date=May 2005 |title=Random matrix theory |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/acta-numerica/article/abs/random-matrix-theory/B291B4E6728E10537C2406CE4C341923 |journal=Acta Numerica |language=en |volume=14 |pages=233–297 |doi=10.1017/S0962492904000236 |bibcode=2005AcNum..14..233E |issn=1474-0508|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Level spacings ===
From ordered eigenvalues <math>\lambda_{1} < \dots < \lambda_{n} < \lambda_{n+1} < \dots < \lambda_{N}</math>, define normalized spacings <math>s_n = \frac{\lambda_{n+1} - \lambda_{n}}{\langle s \rangle}</math> with mean spacing <math>\langle s \rangle</math>. This normalizes the spacings by:<math display="block">\int_{0}^{\infty} p_{\beta}(s) \, ds = 1,\qquad \int_{0}^{\infty} s\, p_{\beta}(s) \, ds = 1,\qquad \beta = 1, 2, 4.</math>With this, the approximate spacing distributions are
<math display="block">p_{\beta}(s) = \begin{cases}
\frac{\pi}{2} s \exp\left(-\frac{\pi}{4} s^{2}\right) & \beta = 1 \\
\frac{32}{\pi^{2}} s^{2} \exp\left(-\frac{4}{\pi} s^{2}\right) & \beta = 2 \\
\frac{2^{18}}{3^{6}\pi^{3}} s^{4} \exp\left(-\frac{64}{9\pi} s^{2}\right) & \beta = 4 \\
\end{cases}</math>

=== Moments ===
For GOE(N), its [[Moment-generating function|moment generating function]] is <math display="inline">\mathbb E\left[e^{\operatorname{Tr}(V W_{N})}\right] = e^{\frac{1}{4}\|V + V^{\text{T}}\|_{F}^{2}}</math>, where <math>\|\cdot\|_{F}</math> is the [[Frobenius norm]].

== Rotationally symmetric ensemble ==
The GUE(N) ensemble can be understood as a particularly representative member of the general family of rotationally symmetric ensembles over Hermitian matrices. The general theory of rotationally symmetric ensembles has allowed researchers to prove some [[Universality class|universality]] results.<ref>{{Citation |last=Bleher |first=Pavel M. |chapter=Lectures on Random Matrix Models |date=2011 |title=Random Matrices, Random Processes and Integrable Systems |pages=251–349 |editor-last=Harnad |editor-first=John |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-9514-8_4 |isbn=978-1-4419-9514-8}}</ref>

== Physics ==

=== The Wigner surmise ===
{{Main|Wigner surmise}}
The Gaussian ensemble was first motivated in theoretical physics. In the 1940s, [[Eugene Wigner]] studied the irregular spacings of slow-[[neutron]] resonances in heavy nuclei. Working with the few dozen levels then available, he noticed a pronounced [[Level repulsion|repulsion between neighbouring lines]].

In 1951, he modelled the Hamiltonian of a [[Compound nucleus|compound-nucleus]] in a minimal way.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wigner |first=Eugene P. |date=October 1951 |title=On the statistical distribution of the widths and spacings of nuclear resonance levels |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/on-the-statistical-distribution-of-the-widths-and-spacings-of-nuclear-resonance-levels/97EAA86F8F11C09D67D47CD700107D34 |journal=Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |language=en |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=790–798 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100027237 |bibcode=1951PCPS...47..790W |issn=1469-8064|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He noted that by symmetry considerations, it must be a real symmetric operator, so he modelled it as a random sample from the GOE(N). He solved the 2×2 case and found the two-level spacing law <math>P(s)=\frac{\pi}{2}s e^{-\pi s^{2}/4}</math>, which matched well with the data. He disseminated his guess ("the Wigner surmise") during a conference on [[Neutron time-of-flight scattering|Neutron Physics by Time-of-Flight]] in 1956:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Conference on Neutron Physics by Time-of-Flight |url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/SCSB-3197271 |title=Conference on Neutron Physics by Time-of-Flight, held at Gatlinburg, Tennessee, November 1 and 2, 1956; Oak Ridge National Laboratory Report ORNL-2309 |publisher=Oak Ridge National Laboratory |year=1957 |page=67 |language=English |orig-date=1956}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Porter |first=Charles E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b2VJAAAACAAJ |title=Statistical Theories of Spectra: Fluctuations |date=1965 |publisher=Elsevier Science & Technology Books |isbn=978-0-12-562356-8 |page=208 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Barrett |first1=Owen |chapter=From Quantum Systems to L-Functions: Pair Correlation Statistics and Beyond |date=2016 |title=Open Problems in Mathematics |pages=123–171 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |arxiv=1505.07481 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-32162-2_2 |isbn=978-3-319-32160-8 |s2cid=33509062 |last2=Firk |first2=Frank W. K. |last3=Miller |first3=Steven J. |last4=Turnage-Butterbaugh |first4=Caroline}}</ref>{{Blockquote|text=Perhaps I am now too courageous when I try to guess the distribution of the distances between successive levels (of energies of heavy nuclei). Theoretically, the situation is quite simple if one attacks the problem in a simpleminded fashion. The question is simply what are the distances of the characteristic values of a symmetric matrix with random coefficients.|title=Results and theory of resonance absorption|author=Eugene Wigner|source=}}Freeman Dyson stated the project as a statistical theory of nuclear energy levels, to be contrasted with precise calculations based on an analytic model of the nucleus. He argued that a statistical theory is necessary, because the energy levels then measured were on the order of millions, and for such a high order, precise calculations was simply impossible. The idea was different from the then-understood form of statistical mechanics, for instead of having a system with precisely stated dynamical laws, with too many particles interacting under it, thus the particles need to be treated statistically, he would model the dynamical laws ''themselves'' as unknown, and thus treated statistically.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dyson |first=Freeman J. |date=1962-01-01 |title=Statistical Theory of the Energy Levels of Complex Systems. I |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/3/1/140/453743/Statistical-Theory-of-the-Energy-Levels-of-Complex |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=140–156 |doi=10.1063/1.1703773 |bibcode=1962JMP.....3..140D |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Threefold Way ===
In 1962, Dyson proposed the "Threefold Way" to motivate the three ensembles, by showing that in 3 fields ([[group representation]], quantum mechanics, random matrix theory), there is a 3-fold disjunction, which he traced back to the [[Frobenius theorem (real division algebras)|Frobenius theorem]] stating that there are only 3 real division algebras: the real, the complex, and the quaternionic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dyson |first=Freeman J. |date=1962-11-01 |title=The Threefold Way. Algebraic Structure of Symmetry Groups and Ensembles in Quantum Mechanics |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/3/6/1199/228285/The-Threefold-Way-Algebraic-Structure-of-Symmetry |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=1199–1215 |doi=10.1063/1.1703863 |bibcode=1962JMP.....3.1199D |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A [[random matrix]] representing a [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] <math>H</math> can be classified by an [[antiunitary operator|anti-unitary]] operator <math>T</math> that describes [[T-symmetry|time-reversal symmetry]]. The classification depends on whether <math>T</math> exists present and, if so, the value of <math>T^2</math>. Each symmetry class produces a constraint on the possible form of <math>H</math>, and the corresponding gaussian ensemble can then be motivated as a maximal entropy distribution, [[Gaussian ensemble#By maximal entropy|as described previously]].

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Dyson's Threefold Way
! Symmetry
! Matrix basis where <math>H</math> is...
!Group representation
! Ensemble
|-
| <math>T^2 = +1</math> (e.g., [[integer spin]], no strong [[spin–orbit interaction]])
| real symmetric
|real
| GOE
|-
| No <math>T</math> (e.g., presence of a [[magnetic field]], magnetic impurities, chiral [[gauge theory|gauge potential]])
| complex Hermitian
|complex
| GUE
|-
| <math>T^2 = -1</math> (e.g., [[half-integer spin]] ''with'' spin-orbit interaction)
| quaternionic self-adjoint (symplectic)
|[[Quaternionic representation|pseudoreal]]
| GSE
|}

If <math>T^2=+1</math>, the Hamiltonian <math>H</math> must be real symmetric. This typically occurs in systems with no [[magnetic field]] and either spinless particles or [[integer spin]] particles with negligible [[spin–orbit interaction]]. This occurs in level spacing distribution in nuclear compound states, the original motivation for Wigner.

If <math>T</math> does not exist, then <math>H</math> is only required to be Hermitian. Time-reversal symmetry can be broken by a homogeneous [[magnetic field]], random magnetic fluxes, or spin-selective [[laser]]s. In these cases, the off-diagonal matrix elements acquire independent complex phases.
* [[Quantum chaos|Chaotic]] microwave cavities with a ferrite: Adding a strong axial magnetic field causes the level statistics to transition continuously from GOE to GUE, which was a confirmation of the [[BGS conjecture]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=So |first1=Paul |last2=Anlage |first2=Steven M. |last3=Ott |first3=Edward |last4=Oerter |first4=Robert N. |date=1995-04-03 |title=Wave Chaos Experiments with and without Time Reversal Symmetry: GUE and GOE Statistics |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.2662 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=74 |issue=14 |pages=2662–2665 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.2662|pmid=10057986 |bibcode=1995PhRvL..74.2662S |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* [[Quantum Hall effect]]: The physics of quantum Hall edge states and [[Landau quantization|Landau levels]] is modelled by the GUE due to the strong perpendicular magnetic field breaking time-reversal symmetry.
* [[Anderson localization]] in 3-D: Applying an [[Aharonov–Bohm effect|Aharonov–Bohm flux]] can drive a system's statistics from GOE to GUE at a disorder-induced metal-insulator transition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Batsch |first1=M. |last2=Schweitzer |first2=L. |last3=Zharekeshev |first3=I. Kh. |last4=Kramer |first4=B. |date=1996-08-19 |title=Crossover from Critical Orthogonal to Critical Unitary Statistics at the Anderson Transition |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.1552 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=77 |issue=8 |pages=1552–1555 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.1552 |pmid=10063107 |arxiv=cond-mat/9607070 |bibcode=1996PhRvL..77.1552B |issn=0031-9007}}</ref>
If <math>T^2=-1</math>, then this is a consequence of [[Kramers' theorem]] for systems with [[half-integer spin]] and significant [[spin–orbit interaction]]. The resulting Hamiltonians are naturally described by [[quaternion]]-Hermitian matrices. It has been observed in Kramers doublet<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rehemanjiang |first1=A. |last2=Allgaier |first2=M. |last3=Joyner |first3=C. H. |last4=Müller |first4=S. |last5=Sieber |first5=M. |last6=Kuhl |first6=U. |last7=Stöckmann |first7=H.-J. |date=2016-08-05 |title=Microwave Realization of the Gaussian Symplectic Ensemble |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.064101 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=117 |issue=6 |article-number=064101 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.064101 |pmid=27541466 |arxiv=1601.00467 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.117f4101R |issn=0031-9007}}</ref> and many quantum chaotic systems. It is also possible to construct such a system without spin.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Joyner |first1=Christopher H. |last2=Müller |first2=Sebastian |last3=Sieber |first3=Martin |date=2014-09-01 |title=GSE statistics without spin |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/107/50004 |journal=EPL (Europhysics Letters) |volume=107 |issue=5 |article-number=50004 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/107/50004 |arxiv=1302.2554 |bibcode=2014EL....10750004J |issn=0295-5075}}</ref>
